See~Creffig:paths-lem for an illustration. Since \[ b+(k-1) cdot p leqslant fracn2k^2 + (k-1) cdot fracn2k^3 leqslant fracnk^2, \] all vertices defined in P_b,s,p do indeed belong to the graph G. Since for different s,s' in [k], the two lines P_b,p,s and P_b,p,s' do not share a vertex, H_b,p will be a vertex-disjoint union of k separate k-cliques. But this contradicts the fact that the edge is inserted by some subgraph other than H_b,p (to violate the inducedness property), concluding the proof.

nodes.statement: Recall that we set k=q/2 above. If x_i=1, then V(H_i) in G contains k disjoint k-cliques in E_A (from H_i) and the edges in E_B fully connect every pair of these cliques, making V(H_i) a k^2-clique in G. Thus, in this case, we have chi(G) geqslant k^2 = q^2/4 by the choice of k. If x_i=0, then by~Creflem:graph-simple, we know that G_A is k-colorable. Since E_B only contains edges between the k vertex-disjoint cliques in V(H_i), G_B is also k-colorable. Moreover, since all edges of H_i are removed from G_A, this means that we can color V(H_i) with k colors (to handle edges E_B) and V setminus V(H_i) with another k colors (to handle edges E_A) and have chi(G) leqslant 2k = q.

Recall that we set $k=q/2$ above. 
     
    If $x_i=1$, then $V(H_i)$ in $G$ contains $k$ disjoint $k$-cliques in $E_A$ (from $H_i$) and the edges in $E_B$ fully connect every pair of these cliques, making $V(H_i)$ a $k^2$-clique in $G$. 
    Thus, in this case, we have $\chi(G) \geqslant k^2 = q^2/4$ by the choice of $k$. 
    
    If $x_i=0$, then by~\Cref{lem:graph-simple}, we know that $G_A$ is $k$-colorable. Since $E_B$ only contains edges between the $k$ vertex-disjoint cliques in $V(H_i)$, $G_B$ is also $k$-colorable. Moreover, since all edges of $H_i$ are removed
    from $G_A$, this means that we can color $V(H_i)$ with $k$ colors (to handle edges $E_B$) and $V \setminus V(H_i)$ with another $k$ colors  (to handle edges $E_A$) and have $\chi(G) \leqslant 2k = q$.

Thus, in this case, we have chi(G) geqslant k^2 = q^2/4 by the choice of k. If x_i=0, then by~Creflem:graph-simple, we know that G_A is k-colorable. Since E_B only contains edges between the k vertex-disjoint cliques in V(H_i), G_B is also k-colorable. Moreover, since all edges of H_i are removed from G_A, this means that we can color V(H_i) with k colors (to handle edges E_B) and V setminus V(H_i) with another k colors (to handle edges E_A) and have chi(G) leqslant 2k = q.

nodes.name: Proof of~\Cref{thm:two-player}
nodes.statement: By~Creflem:two-player-reduction, protocol pi_textscindex outputs the correct answer to the Index problem whenever pi_textsccolor is correct in solving the coloring problem on G = (V, E_A cup E_B), which happens with probability at least 2/3 by the theorem statement. Since CC(pi_textscindex) = CC(pi_textsccolor) on one hand, and CC(pi_textscindex) = Omega(t) by~Crefprop:INDEX-lowerbound, we obtain CC(pi_textsccolor) = Omega(t) also. Finally, since t = Omega(n^2/k^5) = Omega(n^2/q^5) by~Creflem:graph-simple, we can conclude the proof.

By~\Cref{lem:two-player-reduction}, protocol $\pi_{\textsc{index}}$ outputs the correct answer to the Index problem whenever $\pi_{\textsc{color}}$ is correct in solving the coloring problem on $G = (V, E_A \cup E_B)$, 
	which happens with probability at least $2/3$ by the theorem statement. Since $CC(\pi_{\textsc{index}}) = CC(\pi_{\textsc{color}})$ on one hand, and $CC(\pi_{\textsc{index}}) = \Omega(t)$ by~\Cref{prop:INDEX-lowerbound}, 
	we obtain $CC(\pi_{\textsc{color}}) = \Omega(t)$ also. Finally, since $t = \Omega(n^2/k^5) = \Omega(n^2/q^5)$ by~\Cref{lem:graph-simple}, we can conclude the proof.

\label{def:cpg}
	For any $r,t,k \geqslant 1$, an \textbf{$(r,t,k)$-cluster packing} graph is a graph $G=(V,E)$ whose edges can be partitioned into $t$ separate induced $k$-clusters $C_1,\ldots,C_t$, each of size $r$. 
	Throughout, we additionally require a $(r,t,k)$-cluster packing graph to be $k$-colorable\footnote{As we shall show in~\Cref{app:cpg-k-color}, any arbitrary cluster packing graph can be modified to satisfy this requirement with minimal
	 loss in the parameters.}.

Throughout, we additionally require a (r,t,k)-cluster packing graph to be k-colorablefootnoteAs we shall show in~Crefapp:cpg-k-color, any arbitrary cluster packing graph can be modified to satisfy this requirement with minimal loss in the parameters..

nodes.name: Proof of~\Cref{prop:cpg-large-r}
nodes.statement: Start with an empty graph G=(V,E) with n vertices for a sufficiently large n. We start with some parameters and notation for vertices and then define the edges. The reader may want to refer to~Creffig:cpg-large-r for an illustration of different parts of the construction. paragraphParameters, vertices, and their weights and coloring. Fix the following integer parameters \[ d=Theta(fraclog nloglog n) and p:=kcdot d^10, \] where the hidden constant in the Theta-notation for d will be chosen at the end of the proof. Partition vertices of V into k vertex sets Li1,ldots,Lik, referred to as layers, where each Lii := [p]^d. Let F be the collection of subsets S subseteq [d] promised by~Crefclaim:num-of-sets. For each S in F, define a weight function w_S: [p]^d rightarrow ensuremathN over vertices x = (x_1, ldots, x_d) in [p]^d as \[ w_S(x) := sum_i in S x_i. \] Note that cardS leqslant w_S(x) leqslant left|Sright|cdot p. We further partition each layer L_i into p groups based on w_S(x), where for any i in [k] and j in [p-1], we define the group LijSijS as \[ LijSijS := setx in Lii mid j cdot |S| leqslant w_S(x) < (j+1) cdot |S|. \] Next, define a color tuple \[ (c_1~,~ `white'~,~ c_2~,~ `white'~,~ ldots~,~ c_k~,~ `white'), \] where we take `white' and c_1,ldots,c_k to be k distinct colors. Assign colors to the groups in each layer Lii cyclically according to this tuple: color LijSi1S with c_1, LijSi2S with `white', LijSi3S with c_2, and so on until coloring LijSi2k-1S with c_k, LijSi2kS with white, and then repeat the same cycle until all groups in Lii are colored. For any vertex x, let C_S(x) denote the color of x according to the set S. paragraphLines and edges. For a fixed S in F, and every vertex x in Li1 colored c_1 under S, as long as all coordinates of x+ 2kcdot 1_S are at most p, define a line as a tuple of vertices: \[ P_x,S = (y_1, y_2, ldots, y_k), where y_1 := x and y_i+1 := y_i + 2 1_S in Lii+1; \] here, 1_S in \0,1\^d is the indicator vector of S. For a line P_x,S with vertices y_1,ldots,y_k, the color of vertices, with respect to S, will be c_1,ldots,c_k, respectively. Firstly, note that since the lines are only defined when all coordinates of x+ kcdot 2 1_S are at most p, all vertices in P_x,S do belong to the graph. Moreover, since for every i in [k-1], we have w_S(y_i+1) = w_S(y_i) + 2|S|, the group-number of y_i+1 will be two more than the group-number of y_i (as the gap between weight of each group is cardS). As such, since y_1 is colored with c_1 and we cyclically color the vertices of the groups and the path goes through k groups of vertices, we obtain that the coloring of vertices are c_1,ldots,c_k, respectively. rlapnobreak ifvmode relax else ifdimlastskip<1.5em hskip-lastskip hskip1.5em plus0em minus0.5em fi nobreak vrule height0.75em width0.5em depth0.25emfi_textnormal~~Crefobs:colorful-line The edges of the graph are then as follows: for any S in F and any x in Li1 where the line P_x,S is defined, we add all edges between vertices of each P_x,S to turn it into a k-clique. Finally, for any S in F, we define a k-cluster H_S as the set of all k-cliques obtained from all qualifying lines P_x,S. The fact that H_S is a k-cluster is because the lines P_x,S for different x, by definition, do not share vertices. In the following, we prove a lower bound on the size of these k-clusters and show their inducedness in the graph and then conclude the proof. [h!] includegraphics[width=0.56textwidth]Figs/dense-construction.pdf captionAn illustration of the construction of the cluster packing graph in~Crefprop:cpg-large-r for k=4 and a coloring of vertices in the layers based on a fixed set S. The colors used in the definition of the construction are c_1 (red), c_2 (blue), c_3 (green), c_4 (yellow), and `white'. The thick lines represent the cliques in H_S. An edge corresponding to the dashed line would break the inducedness of the subgraph H_S, but it cannot exist as in any other subgraph H_T for T neq S, there are no lines between a vertex of color c_2 (blue) to any color c_3 (green) vertex (the coloring here is still with respect to S and not T). paragraphSize of k-clusters. The following claim lower bounds the size of each k-cluster defined in G. For a fixed Sin F, the number of distinct lines P_x, S is at least fracn2k^2 cdot (1-o(1)). The number of P_x,S lines depends on the number of vertices in Li1 that are colored c_1 and satisfy x_i +2k leqslant p for all i in S. The total number of distinct weights is cardS cdot (p-1) + 1, hence the number of groups in Li1 is at most p. Since the color c_1 appears in Li1 once every 2k groups, the number of c_1-colored groups is at least fracp-12k - 1, so the proportion of c_1-colored groups is at least fracfracp-12k-1p=frac12k cdot (1-o(1)). tagsince p gg k The total number of vertices in L_1 is p^d. The number of vertices with all coordinates in S smaller than p-2k is at least (p - 2k)^d. Hence, the proportion of such vertices is at least frac(p-2k)^dp^d &=left(1-frac2kpright)^d simeq expleft(-frac2kcdot dkcdot d^10right) tagusing 1-xsimeq e^-x\\ & simeq 1-frac2kcdot dkcdot d^10 = 1-frac2d^9 = 1- o(frac1k) tagusing p = k cdot d^10 and d > k. Therefore, given n= k cdot p^d and cardL_1=p^k, the number of qualifying lines is at least \[ fracp^d2k cdot paren1-o(1) - o(fracp^dk) geqslant fracn2k^2 cdot paren1-o(1), \] completing the proof. rlapnobreak ifvmode relax else ifdimlastskip<1.5em hskip-lastskip hskip1.5em plus0em minus0.5em fi nobreak vrule height0.75em width0.5em depth0.25emfi_textnormal~~Crefclaim:lower-bound-r paragraphInducedness. The following claim shows that every k-cluster H_S is induced in G. For each Sin F, the induced subgraph of G on V(H_S) only contains edges of H_S. Fix some S in F and suppose by contradiction that there exists an edge (u, v) in V(H_S) which is not part of H_S itself. By construction, such an edge could only exist if both u and v lie on the same line P_z, T for some z in Li1, T neq S in F (so are added as part of H_T). Assume u in Lii and v in Lij with i neq j (since there are no intra-layer edges). By~Crefobs:colorful-line, we have C_S(u)=c_i and C_S(v)=c_j, therefore there exist integers alpha and beta such that (2kcdot alpha+2(i-1)) cardS &leqslant w_S(u) < (2kcdotalpha+2(i-1)+1) cardS; \\ (2kcdotbeta+2(j-1)) cardS &leqslant w_S(v) < (2kcdotbeta+2(j-1)+1) cardS. This is by the cyclic coloring of groups in each layer and the definition of each group. Assume i<j, then with u, v in P_z, T, we have v=u+2(j-i) 1_T. Therefore, \[ w_S(v)= w_S(u+2(j-i) 1_T)= w_S(u) + w_S(2(j-i) 1_T) geqslant w_S(u). \] Using w_S(v) geqslant w_S(u), and as the weight range for different groups have no overlap, we have 2kcdotbeta+2(j-1) geqslant 2kcdot alpha+2(i-1)+1 (and consequently, betageqslant alpha). Then, with respect to the weights on set S: w_S(v-u) &= w_S(v) - w_S(u) \\ &geqslant (2kcdotbeta+2(j-1))left|Sright| - (2kcdotalpha+2(i-1)+1)left| S right| \\ &= cardScdot paren2kcdot(beta-alpha)+2(j-i)-1\\ &= fracd3 cdot paren2kcdot(beta-alpha)+2(j-i)-1 tagas cardS = d/3 \\ &geqslant fracd3 cdot paren2(j-i)-1 tagsince betageqslant alpha \\ &geqslant fracd3 cdot (j-i) tagsince cardj-igeqslant 1 intertext On the other hand, as u, v in P_z, T, we have v=u+2(j-i) 1_T. Therefore, w_S(v-u) &= w_S(2(j-i) cdot 1_T)= 2(j-i)cdot w_S(1_T) = 2(j-i)cdotcardScap T \\ &leqslant 2(j-i)cdot fracd7 < fracd3 cdot (j-i), a contradiction (as the lower bound in RHS of first equation is larger than the upper bound of the second). Hence, the edge (u,v) cannot exist, proving the inducedness property. rlapnobreak ifvmode relax else ifdimlastskip<1.5em hskip-lastskip hskip1.5em plus0em minus0.5em fi nobreak vrule height0.75em width0.5em depth0.25emfi_textnormal~~Crefclaim:H_S-induced paragraphConcluding the proof. To conclude, by~Crefclaim:lower-bound-r and~Crefclaim:H_S-induced, we already established that G is a (r,t,k)-cluster packing graph with parameters \[ r = fracn2k^2 cdot (1-o(1)) and t = 2^Omega(d) = n^Theta(frac1loglogn); \] we only need to ensure that we can pick d to be in Theta(logn/loglogn) as required by our proof. By the construction of the graph and choice of parameter p, we have \[ n = k cdot p^d = k cdot parenk cdot d^10^d = k^d+1 cdot d^10d. \] Since k = o(logn/loglogn) in the theorem statement, we can set d to be some fixed choice in Theta(logn/loglogn) and ensure the above equation holds, concluding the proof. rlapnobreak ifvmode relax else ifdimlastskip<1.5em hskip-lastskip hskip1.5em plus0em minus0.5em fi nobreak vrule height0.75em width0.5em depth0.25emfi_textnormal~~Crefprop:cpg-large-r

By construction, such an edge could only exist if both u and v lie on the same line P_z, T for some z in Li1, T neq S in F (so are added as part of H_T). Assume u in Lii and v in Lij with i neq j (since there are no intra-layer edges). By~Crefobs:colorful-line, we have C_S(u)=c_i and C_S(v)=c_j, therefore there exist integers alpha and beta such that (2kcdot alpha+2(i-1)) cardS &leqslant w_S(u) < (2kcdotalpha+2(i-1)+1) cardS; \\ (2kcdotbeta+2(j-1)) cardS &leqslant w_S(v) < (2kcdotbeta+2(j-1)+1) cardS. This is by the cyclic coloring of groups in each layer and the definition of each group. Assume i<j, then with u, v in P_z, T, we have v=u+2(j-i) 1_T. Therefore, \[ w_S(v)= w_S(u+2(j-i) 1_T)= w_S(u) + w_S(2(j-i) 1_T) geqslant w_S(u). \] Using w_S(v) geqslant w_S(u), and as the weight range for different groups have no overlap, we have 2kcdotbeta+2(j-1) geqslant 2kcdot alpha+2(i-1)+1 (and consequently, betageqslant alpha). Therefore, w_S(v-u) &= w_S(2(j-i) cdot 1_T)= 2(j-i)cdot w_S(1_T) = 2(j-i)cdotcardScap T \\ &leqslant 2(j-i)cdot fracd7 < fracd3 cdot (j-i), a contradiction (as the lower bound in RHS of first equation is larger than the upper bound of the second). Hence, the edge (u,v) cannot exist, proving the inducedness property. rlapnobreak ifvmode relax else ifdimlastskip<1.5em hskip-lastskip hskip1.5em plus0em minus0.5em fi nobreak vrule height0.75em width0.5em depth0.25emfi_textnormal~~Crefclaim:H_S-induced

Fix some $S \in \mathcal{F}$ and suppose by contradiction that there exists an edge $(u, v)$ in $V(H_S)$ which is not part of $H_S$ itself.  
        By construction, such an edge could only exist if both $u$ and $v$ lie on the same line $P_{z, T}$ for some $z \in \Li{1}$, $T \neq S \in \mathcal{F}$ (so are added as part of $H_T$).
        Assume $u \in \Li{i}$ and $v \in \Li{j}$ with $i \neq j$ (since there are no intra-layer edges). 
        By~\Cref{obs:colorful-line}, we have $C_S(u)=c_i$ and $C_S(v)=c_j$, therefore there exist integers $\alpha$ and $\beta$ such that
         \begin{align*}
         (2k\cdot \alpha+2(i-1)) \card{S} &\leqslant w_S(u) < (2k\cdot\alpha+2(i-1)+1) \card{S};
         \\
         (2k\cdot\beta+2(j-1)) \card{S} &\leqslant w_S(v) < (2k\cdot\beta+2(j-1)+1) \card{S}.
         \end{align*}
         This is by the cyclic coloring of groups in each layer and the definition of each group. 
         Assume $i<j$, then with $u, v \in P_{z, T}$, we have $v=u+2(j-i) \mathbf{1}_T$. Therefore,
         \[
         w_S(v)= w_S(u+2(j-i) \mathbf{1}_T)= w_S(u) + w_S(2(j-i) \mathbf{1}_T) \geqslant w_S(u).
         \]
         Using $w_S(v) \geqslant w_S(u$), and as the weight range for different groups have no overlap, we have
         $2k\cdot\beta+2(j-1) \geqslant 2k\cdot \alpha+2(i-1)+1$ (and consequently, $\beta\geqslant \alpha$). Then, with respect to the weights on set $S$:
        \begin{align*}
            w_S(v-u) 
            &= w_S(v) - w_S(u)
            \\
            &\geqslant (2k\cdot\beta+2(j-1))\left|S\right| - (2k\cdot\alpha+2(i-1)+1)\left| S \right| \\
            &= \card{S}\cdot \paren{2k\cdot(\beta-\alpha)+2(j-i)-1}\\
            &= \frac{d}{3} \cdot \paren{2k\cdot(\beta-\alpha)+2(j-i)-1} \tag{as $\card{S} = d/3$} \\
            &\geqslant \frac{d}{3} \cdot \paren{2(j-i)-1} \tag{since $\beta\geqslant \alpha$} \\
            &\geqslant \frac{d}{3} \cdot (j-i) \tag{since $\card{j-i}\geqslant 1$} 
        \intertext{
        On the other hand, as $u, v \in P_{z, T}$, we have $v=u+2(j-i) \mathbf{1}_T$. Therefore, 
        }
             w_S(v-u) &= w_S(2(j-i) \cdot \mathbf{1}_T)= 2(j-i)\cdot { w_S(\mathbf{1}_T)} = {2(j-i)}\cdot\card{S\cap T} \\ 
            &\leqslant {2(j-i)}\cdot \frac{d}{7} < \frac{d}{3} \cdot (j-i), 
        \end{align*}
        a contradiction (as the lower bound in RHS of first equation is larger than the upper bound of the second). Hence, the edge $(u,v)$ cannot exist, proving the inducedness property. \rlap{\nobreak \ifvmode \relax \else \ifdim\lastskip<1.5em \hskip-\lastskip \hskip1.5em plus0em minus0.5em \fi \nobreak \vrule height0.75em width0.5em depth0.25em\fi$_{\textnormal{~~\Cref{claim:H_S-induced}}}$}

We prove this claim by induction on $p$.
		For the base case where $p=2$, by~\Cref{obs:two-player-clique} we know the claim holds.
		
		Suppose the statement holds for $p-1$. We know that $\ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{ans}}}(G_{p-1}) = \ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{ans}}}(G)$ also by construction.

		If $\ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{ans}}}(G)=1$, by the induction hypothesis, the vertices in $\ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{spec}}}(G_{p-1})$ form a $k^{p-1}$-clique.  Mapping $\sigma$ is chosen so that each vertex of this clique corresponds to one of the sets in $\{\cliqnum{\ensuremath{i^{\star}}}{j} \mid j \in S_{\ensuremath{i^{\star}}} \cap T\}$. We know that $\ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{spec}}}(G) = \cup_{j \in S_{\ensuremath{i^{\star}}} \cap T} \cliqnum{\ensuremath{i^{\star}}}{j}$, thus all vertices inside $\cliqnum{\ensuremath{i^{\star}}}{j}$ are connected to all vertices inside $\cliqnum{\ensuremath{i^{\star}}}{j'}$ for all $j, j' \in S_{\ensuremath{i^{\star}}} \cap T$ and $j \neq j'$ by the clique join operation in step \ref{part:hard-inst-cliqjoin} of \Cref{distpart:hard-instance}. On the other hand, as $\ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{ans}}}(G)=1$, all the edges inside each clique $\cliqnum{\ensuremath{i^{\star}}}{j}$ for $j \in S_{\ensuremath{i^{\star}}} \cap T$ are added by $E_1$ given to $\player{1}$. Therefore, all the vertices inside $\ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{spec}}}(G)$ are connected and form a $k^p$-clique, resulting in $\chi(G)\geqslant k^p$. 


 		If $\ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{ans}}}(G)=0$, by induction we know $\chi(G_{p-1})\leqslant k\cdot (p-1)$. Properly color $G_{p-1}$ using $k\cdot (p-1)$ colors and use the mapping $\sigma$ to color the corresponding vertices in $\bigcup_{j\in T} C_j^{(i^*)}$ with the same colors. As $\ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{ans}}}(G)=0$, each vertex $\sigma(v)$ is mapped to a clique $\cliqnum{i^*}{j}$ for $j \in T$, and no edges inside these cliques are added by $E_1$. We have constructed the hard distributions $\{\ensuremath{\mathcal{G}}_a\}_{2 \leqslant a \leqslant p}$ based on the cluster packing graphs given in the statement of the lemma. 
	
	Now, let us assume towards a contradiction that there exists a deterministic $p$-player protocol $\ensuremath{\pi}$ that distinguishes between $\ensuremath{\chi}(G) \leqslant k \cdot p$ and $\ensuremath{\chi}(G) > k^p$ for graphs $G \sim \ensuremath{\mathcal{G}}_p(n_p, k)$ with probability of success at least $2/3$.
	By~\Cref{clm:ans-to-chromatic}, this protocol can also find the value of $\ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{ans}}}(G)$ as  $\ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{ans}}}(G) = 0$ when $\ensuremath{\chi}(G) \leqslant k \cdot p$ and $\ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{ans}}}(G) = 1$ when $\ensuremath{\chi}(G) > k^p$. Thus, the success probability of $\ensuremath{\pi}$ in correctly computing $\ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{ans}}}(G)$ is at least:
	\[
		\frac23 \geqslant \frac12 + \frac{p}{6(p+1)}.
	\]
	
	Therefore, by~\Cref{lem:inductive-hardness-Gp}, the communication cost of $\ensuremath{\pi}$ must be at least 
	\[
		s_p(n_p) = \min\Big\{\frac{c \cdot r_p \cdot t_p}{k^{(p-1)} \cdot (p+1)^2}, s_{p-1}(n_{p-1})\Big\}  = \underset{2 \leqslant a \leqslant p}{\min}\Big \{ \frac{c \cdot r_a \cdot t_a}{(a+1)^2 \cdot k^{a-1}}\Big\},
	\]
	where the equality follows from expanding the recursion for $s_{p-1}(n_{p-1})$ down to $p = 2$.

We prove \Cref{clm:dist-close-fake} using the data processing inequality for total variation distance, from \Cref{fact:tvd-data-processing} and the weak chain rule from \Cref{fact:tvd-chain-rule}. 
		\begin{align*}
			&\tvd{\ensuremath{\mathcal{G}^{\textnormal{real}}}_p(\ \ensuremath{\rv{\ensuremath{\Pi}}}_1, \ensuremath{\rv{T}}, \ensuremath{\rv{i}^{\star}}, \ensuremath{\bm{\sigma}}, \ensuremath{\rv{G}}_{p-1})}{\ensuremath{\mathcal{G}^{\textnormal{fake}}}_p(\ensuremath{\rv{\ensuremath{\Pi}}}_1, \ensuremath{\rv{T}}, \ensuremath{\rv{i}^{\star}}, \ensuremath{\bm{\sigma}}, \ensuremath{\rv{G}}_{p-1})} \\
			&\leqslant \tvd{\ensuremath{\mathcal{G}^{\textnormal{real}}}_p( \ensuremath{\rv{\ensuremath{\Pi}}}_1, \ensuremath{\rv{T}}, \ensuremath{\rv{i}^{\star}}, \ensuremath{\bm{\sigma}})}{\ensuremath{\mathcal{G}^{\textnormal{fake}}}_p(\ensuremath{\rv{\ensuremath{\Pi}}}_1, \ensuremath{\rv{T}}, \ensuremath{\rv{i}^{\star}}, \ensuremath{\bm{\sigma}})} \\
			&\hspace{4mm} + \ensuremath{{\mathbb{E}}}_{ (\ensuremath{\rv{\ensuremath{\Pi}}}_1, \ensuremath{\rv{T}}, \ensuremath{\rv{i}^{\star}}, \ensuremath{\bm{\sigma}}) \sim \ensuremath{\mathcal{G}^{\textnormal{real}}}_p} \tvd{\ensuremath{\mathcal{G}^{\textnormal{real}}}_p(\ensuremath{\rv{G}}_{p-1} \mid  \ensuremath{\rv{\ensuremath{\Pi}}}_1, \ensuremath{\rv{T}}, \ensuremath{\rv{i}^{\star}}, \ensuremath{\bm{\sigma}})}{\ensuremath{\mathcal{G}^{\textnormal{fake}}}_p(\ensuremath{\rv{G}}_{p-1} \mid \ensuremath{\rv{\ensuremath{\Pi}}}_1, \ensuremath{\rv{T}}, \ensuremath{\rv{i}^{\star}}, \ensuremath{\bm{\sigma}})} \tag{by \Cref{fact:tvd-chain-rule}} \\
			&= 0 + \ensuremath{{\mathbb{E}}}_{ (\ensuremath{\rv{\ensuremath{\Pi}}}_1, \ensuremath{\rv{T}}, \ensuremath{\rv{i}^{\star}}, \ensuremath{\bm{\sigma}}) \sim \ensuremath{\mathcal{G}}_p} \tvd{\ensuremath{\mathcal{G}^{\textnormal{real}}}_p(\ensuremath{\rv{G}}_{p-1} \mid  \ensuremath{\rv{\ensuremath{\Pi}}}_1, \ensuremath{\rv{T}}, \ensuremath{\rv{i}^{\star}}, \ensuremath{\bm{\sigma}})}{\ensuremath{\mathcal{G}^{\textnormal{fake}}}_p(\ensuremath{\rv{G}}_{p-1} \mid \ensuremath{\rv{\ensuremath{\Pi}}}_1, \ensuremath{\rv{T}}, \ensuremath{\rv{i}^{\star}}, \ensuremath{\bm{\sigma}})} \tag{by definition of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{G}^{\textnormal{fake}}}_p$} \\
			&= \ensuremath{{\mathbb{E}}}_{ (\ensuremath{\rv{\ensuremath{\Pi}}}_1, \ensuremath{\rv{T}}, \ensuremath{\rv{i}^{\star}}, \ensuremath{\bm{\sigma}}) \sim \ensuremath{\mathcal{G}}_p} \tvd{\ensuremath{\mathcal{G}^{\textnormal{real}}}_p(\ensuremath{\rv{G}}_{p-1} \mid  \ensuremath{\rv{\ensuremath{\Pi}}}_1, \ensuremath{\rv{T}}, \ensuremath{\rv{i}^{\star}}, \ensuremath{\bm{\sigma}})}{\ensuremath{\mathcal{G}^{\textnormal{fake}}}_p(\ensuremath{\rv{G}}_{p-1})},
		\end{align*}
		as in $\ensuremath{\mathcal{G}^{\textnormal{fake}}}_p$, distribution of $\ensuremath{\rv{G}}_{p-1}$ is chosen independently from all other random variables. 
		We continue as, 
		\begin{align*}
			& \ensuremath{{\mathbb{E}}}_{ (\ensuremath{\rv{\ensuremath{\Pi}}}_1, \ensuremath{\rv{T}}, \ensuremath{\rv{i}^{\star}}, \ensuremath{\bm{\sigma}}) \sim \ensuremath{\mathcal{G}}_p} \tvd{\ensuremath{\mathcal{G}^{\textnormal{real}}}_p(\ensuremath{\rv{G}}_{p-1} \mid  \ensuremath{\rv{\ensuremath{\Pi}}}_1, \ensuremath{\rv{T}}, \ensuremath{\rv{i}^{\star}}, \ensuremath{\bm{\sigma}})}{\ensuremath{\mathcal{G}^{\textnormal{fake}}}_p(\ensuremath{\rv{G}}_{p-1})}\\
			&\leqslant \ensuremath{{\mathbb{E}}}_{ (\ensuremath{\rv{\ensuremath{\Pi}}}_1, \ensuremath{\rv{T}}, \ensuremath{\rv{i}^{\star}}, \ensuremath{\bm{\sigma}}) \sim \ensuremath{\mathcal{G}}_p} \tvd{\ensuremath{\mathcal{G}^{\textnormal{real}}}_p(\ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{ans}}}(G_{p-1}), \ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{spec}}}(G_{p-1}) \mid  \ensuremath{\rv{\ensuremath{\Pi}}}_1, \ensuremath{\rv{T}}, \ensuremath{\rv{i}^{\star}}, \ensuremath{\bm{\sigma}})}{\ensuremath{\mathcal{G}^{\textnormal{fake}}}_p(\ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{ans}}}(G_{p-1}), \ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{spec}}}(G_{p-1}))},  
		\end{align*}
		where we have used \Cref{fact:tvd-data-processing}, as $\ensuremath{\rv{G}}_{p-1}$ is sampled only based on $\ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{ans}}}(G_{p-1}), \ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{spec}}}(G_{p-1})$ when conditioned on $\ensuremath{\bm{\sigma}}$ in \Cref{distpart:hard-instance} of distribution $\ensuremath{\mathcal{G}^{\textnormal{real}}}_p$. 
		Next, we have, 
		\begin{align*}

Hence, &ensuremathtextnormalPr[ensuremathpi_p-1 textnormal succeeds on G_p-1] \\ &geqslant frac12 + fracp6(p+1) - tvdensuremathG^textnormalreal(ensuremathrvensuremathPi)ensuremathG^textnormalfake(ensuremathrvensuremathPi) tagby Crefeq:interim-pe-1 and Crefeq:interim-pe-2 \\ &geqslant frac12 + fracp6(p+1) - tvdensuremathG^textnormalreal(ensuremathrvensuremathPi_1, ensuremathrvT, ensuremathrvi^star, ensuremathbmsigma, ensuremathrvG_p-1)ensuremathG^textnormalfake(ensuremathrvensuremathPi_1, ensuremathrvT, ensuremathrvi^star, ensuremathbmsigma, ensuremathrvG_p-1) tagas ensuremathpi is deterministic and ensuremathPi is a function of ensuremathrvensuremathPi_1, ensuremathrvT, ensuremathrvi^star, ensuremathbmsigma and ensuremathrvG_p-1, and by Creffact:tvd-data-processing \\ &geqslant frac12 + fracp6(p+1) - frac16(p+1)^2 tagby Crefclm:dist-close-fake\\ &geqslant frac12 + fracp-16p. tagfor any p geqslant 0 By the easy direction of Yao's minimax principle (namely, an averaging argument), protocol ensuremathpi_p-1 can be made deterministic by choosing an appropriate random string so that we get a deterministic protocol with the same probability of success. nodes.raw_latex:
We pick constant $c$ as the minimum of $c_2 $ from \Cref{clm:two-player-basecase} and $\ensuremath{c_{\textnormal{msg}}}$ from \Cref{lem:first-msg}.
		We prove the lemma by induction on $p$. \Cref{clm:two-player-basecase} serves as the base case when $p = 2$, as our choice of constant $c \leqslant c_2$. We assume that the statement is true for $p-1$ as the induction hypothesis. 
		
		Assume towards a contradiction that there exists a deterministic protocol $\ensuremath{\pi}$ where $\player{p}$ outputs the value of $\ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{ans}}}(G)$ with probability at least $\frac12 + \frac{p}{6(p+1)}$ with communication less than
		\[
			 \frac{c \cdot r_p \cdot t_p}{k^{(p-1)} \cdot (p+1)^2}. 
		\]
		\Cref{clm:dist-close-fake} holds with the upper bound on the communication of $\ensuremath{\pi}$, and as $c \leqslant \ensuremath{c_{\textnormal{msg}}}$. 
		We analyze the probability of success for protocol $\ensuremath{\pi}_{p-1}$ on some graph $G_{p-1} \sim \ensuremath{\mathcal{G}}_{p-1}(n_{p-1}, k)$. 
		\begin{align}
			&\ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[\ensuremath{\pi}_{p-1} \textnormal{ succeeds on $G_{p-1}$}] \notag\\
			&\geqslant \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[\ensuremath{\pi}_{p-1} \textnormal{ succeeds on $\ensuremath{\mathcal{G}^{\textnormal{real}}}$}] - \tvd{\ensuremath{\mathcal{G}^{\textnormal{real}}}(\ensuremath{\rv{\ensuremath{\Pi}}})}{\ensuremath{\mathcal{G}^{\textnormal{fake}}}(\ensuremath{\rv{\ensuremath{\Pi}}})}, \label{eq:interim-pe-1}
		\end{align}
		where we have used \Cref{fact:tvd-small} on the event that the protocol succeeds on the two distributions $\ensuremath{\mathcal{G}^{\textnormal{real}}}$ and $\ensuremath{\mathcal{G}^{\textnormal{fake}}} $ of the transcript. 
		
		We know by our assumption that, 
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:interim-pe-2}
		 \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[\ensuremath{\pi}_{p-1} \textnormal{ succeeds on $\ensuremath{\mathcal{G}^{\textnormal{real}}}$}]  \geqslant \frac12 + \frac{p}{6(p+1)},
		\end{equation}
		as the joint distribution of $G_{p-1}, \ensuremath{\Pi}_1, T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}$, and $ \sigma$ that $\ensuremath{\pi}_{p-1}$ runs $\ensuremath{\pi}$ on would be the same as if the input was sampled from  $\ensuremath{\mathcal{G}}_p(n_p,k)$. As $\ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{ans}}}(G) = \ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{ans}}}(G_{p-1})$, $\ensuremath{\pi}_{p-1}$ outputs the correct answer whenever $\ensuremath{\pi}$ is correct. 
		Hence,
		\begin{align*}
				&\ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[\ensuremath{\pi}_{p-1} \textnormal{ succeeds on $G_{p-1}$}] \\ 
				&\geqslant \frac12 + \frac{p}{6(p+1)} -  \tvd{\ensuremath{\mathcal{G}^{\textnormal{real}}}(\ensuremath{\rv{\ensuremath{\Pi}}})}{\ensuremath{\mathcal{G}^{\textnormal{fake}}}(\ensuremath{\rv{\ensuremath{\Pi}}})} \tag{by \Cref{eq:interim-pe-1} and \Cref{eq:interim-pe-2}} \\
				&\geqslant  \frac12 + \frac{p}{6(p+1)} -  \tvd{\ensuremath{\mathcal{G}^{\textnormal{real}}}(\ensuremath{\rv{\ensuremath{\Pi}}}_1, \ensuremath{\rv{T}}, \ensuremath{\rv{i}^{\star}}, \ensuremath{\bm{\sigma}}, \ensuremath{\rv{G}}_{p-1})}{\ensuremath{\mathcal{G}^{\textnormal{fake}}}(\ensuremath{\rv{\ensuremath{\Pi}}}_1, \ensuremath{\rv{T}}, \ensuremath{\rv{i}^{\star}}, \ensuremath{\bm{\sigma}}, \ensuremath{\rv{G}}_{p-1})} \tag{as $\ensuremath{\pi}$ is deterministic and $\ensuremath{\Pi}$ is a function of $\ensuremath{\rv{\ensuremath{\Pi}}}_1, \ensuremath{\rv{T}}, \ensuremath{\rv{i}^{\star}}, \ensuremath{\bm{\sigma}}$ and $\ensuremath{\rv{G}}_{p-1}$, and by \Cref{fact:tvd-data-processing}} \\
				&\geqslant    \frac12 +  \frac{p}{6(p+1)} - \frac1{6(p+1)^2} \tag{by \Cref{clm:dist-close-fake}}\\
				&\geqslant \frac12 + \frac{p-1}{6p}. \tag{for any $p \geqslant 0$}
		\end{align*}

	By the easy direction of Yao's minimax principle (namely, an averaging argument), protocol $\ensuremath{\pi}_{p-1}$ can be made deterministic by choosing an appropriate random string so that we get a deterministic protocol with the same probability of success. The communication cost of $\ensuremath{\pi}_{p-1}$ is at most that of $\ensuremath{\pi}$, as the players only send messages by running $\ensuremath{\pi}$. 
	
	By the induction hypothesis, we get that, $\ensuremath{\pi}_{p-1}$ (and thus $\ensuremath{\pi}$) has communciation cost at least $s_{p-1}(n_{p-1})$. 
	To conclude the proof, either the premise of \Cref{clm:dist-close-fake} does not hold, which implies
	\[
		s_p(n_p) >  \frac{c \cdot r_p \cdot t_p}{k^{(p-1)} \cdot (p+1)^2},
	\]
	or we have shown that if \Cref{clm:dist-close-fake} holds, then,
	\[
		s_p(n_{p}) > s_{p-1}(n_{p-1}). 
	\]
	In either case, we have that, for any $p > 2$, 
	\[
	 s_p(n_p) = \min\Big\{\frac{c \cdot r_p \cdot t_p}{k^{(p-1)} \cdot (p+1)^2}, s_{p-1}(n_{p-1})\Big\} ,
	\]
	completing the proof.

\label{obs:feasible-pair}
		For any choice of $\ensuremath{\Pi}$, $T$ and $\ensuremath{i^{\star}}$, we have the following:
		\begin{enumerate}[label=$(\roman*)$]
			\item The distribution of $\ensuremath{\bm{\sigma}}$ is independent of $\ensuremath{\rv{\ensuremath{\Pi}}}_1$ conditioned on $\ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{spec}}}(G), T$ and $\ensuremath{i^{\star}}$. 
			\item The value of $\ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[\sigma \mid \ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{spec}}}(G) = W, T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}]$ is zero for all $\sigma $ which is not feasible with $W$, and is uniform over all $\sigma$ feasible with $W$. 
			\item For every $W \subset T$ of size $k^{p-1}$, the number of mappings $\sigma$ feasible with $W$ is independent of $W$, and is a fixed number.
			\item Conditioned on $T$, $\sigma$ and $\ensuremath{i^{\star}}$, the value of $\ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{spec}}}(G)$ is uniform over all $W$ feasible with $\sigma$.  
		\end{enumerate}

Let us fix an arbitrary choice of $\ensuremath{\Pi}_1$, $T$ and $\ensuremath{i^{\star}}$. 
		\begin{align*}
			&\ensuremath{{\mathbb{E}}}_{\sigma \mid \ensuremath{\Pi}_1, T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}}	\tvd{\ensuremath{\mathcal{G}}_p(\ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{spec}}}(G) \mid \ensuremath{\Pi}_1, T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}},\sigma)}{\ensuremath{\mathcal{G}}_p(\ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{spec}}}(G) \mid T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}, \sigma)} \\
			&= \sum_{\sigma} \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[\sigma \mid \ensuremath{\Pi}_1, T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}] \cdot \paren{	\tvd{\ensuremath{\mathcal{G}}_p(\ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{spec}}}(G) \mid \ensuremath{\Pi}_1, T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}},\sigma)}{\ensuremath{\mathcal{G}}_p(\ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{spec}}}(G) \mid T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}, \sigma)}} \\
			&=\frac12 \cdot \sum_{\sigma} \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[\sigma \mid \ensuremath{\Pi}_1, T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}] \cdot \sum_{W \in \ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{feas}}}(\sigma)} \card{\ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[W \mid \ensuremath{\Pi}_1, T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}, \sigma] - \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[W \mid T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}, \sigma ]} \tag{by definition of total variation distance} \\
			&= \frac12 \cdot \sum_{\sigma} \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[\sigma \mid \ensuremath{\Pi}_1, T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}] \cdot \sum_{W \in \ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{feas}}}(\sigma)} \card{\ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[W \mid \ensuremath{\Pi}_1, T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}] \cdot \frac{\ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[\sigma \mid \ensuremath{\Pi}_1, T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}, W]}{\ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[\sigma \mid \ensuremath{\Pi}_1, T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}]} - \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[W \mid T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}, \sigma ]}  \\
			&= \frac12 \cdot \sum_{\sigma} \sum_{W \in \ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{feas}}}(\sigma)} \card{\ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[W \mid \ensuremath{\Pi}_1, T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}] \cdot \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[\sigma \mid T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}, W]- \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[W \mid T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}, \sigma ] \cdot \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[\sigma \mid \ensuremath{\Pi}_1, T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}] }. \tag{by part $(i)$ of \Cref{obs:feasible-pair}}
		\end{align*}
		Let $\ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[\sigma \mid T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}, W] = x $ for some $x \in [0,1]$ when $W \in \ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{feas}}}(\sigma)$. By part $(ii)$ and $(iii)$ of \Cref{obs:feasible-pair}, such a value of $x$ exists. 
		\begin{align*}
			\ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[\sigma \mid \ensuremath{\Pi}_1, T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}] = \sum_{W \in \ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{feas}}}(\sigma)} \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[W \mid \ensuremath{\Pi}_1, T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}] \cdot \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[\sigma \mid W, \ensuremath{\Pi}_1, T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}] = \sum_{W \in \ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{feas}}}(\sigma)} \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[W \mid \ensuremath{\Pi}_1, T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}] \cdot x. 
		\end{align*}
		We use $\beta_{\sigma}$ to denote the following:
		\[
		\beta_{\sigma}:= \sum_{W \in \ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{feas}}}(\sigma)} \card{\ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[W \mid \ensuremath{\Pi}_1, T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}] - \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[W \mid T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}]}.
		\]
		We can continue the proof as, 
		\begin{align*}
			&\ensuremath{{\mathbb{E}}}_{\sigma \mid \ensuremath{\Pi}_1, T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}}	\tvd{\ensuremath{\mathcal{G}}_p(\ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{spec}}}(G) \mid \ensuremath{\Pi}_1, T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}},\sigma)}{\ensuremath{\mathcal{G}}_p(\ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{spec}}}(G) \mid T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}, \sigma)} \\
			&= \frac{x}2 \cdot  \sum_{\sigma} \sum_{W \in \ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{feas}}}(\sigma)} \card{\ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[W \mid \ensuremath{\Pi}_1, T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}]- \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[W \mid T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}, \sigma ] \cdot \paren{ \sum_{W \in \ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{feas}}}(\sigma)} \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[W \mid \ensuremath{\Pi}_1, T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}]}} \\
			&\leqslant  \frac{x}2 \cdot  \sum_{\sigma} \sum_{W \in \ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{feas}}}(\sigma)} \Bigg(\card{\ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[W \mid \ensuremath{\Pi}_1, T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}]- \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[W \mid T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}]}\\
			&\hspace{6mm} + \card{\ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[W \mid T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}, \sigma ] \cdot \paren{ \sum_{W \in \ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{feas}}}(\sigma)} \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[W \mid \ensuremath{\Pi}_1, T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}]} - \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[W \mid T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}]}\Bigg) \tag{by triangle inequality}\\
			&\leqslant \frac{x}2 \cdot \sum_{\sigma} \beta_{\sigma} +  \sum_{W \in \ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{feas}}}(\sigma)}\card{\frac1{\card{\ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{feas}}}(\sigma)}} \cdot \paren{ \sum_{W \in \ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{feas}}}(\sigma)} \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[W \mid \ensuremath{\Pi}_1, T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}]} - \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[W \mid T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}]} \tag{by part $(iv)$ of \Cref{obs:feasible-pair}, and definition of $\beta_\sigma$} \\
			&\leqslant \frac{x}2 \cdot \sum_{\sigma} \beta_{\sigma}	+ \frac1{\card{\ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{feas}}}(\sigma)}} \cdot\sum_{W \in \ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{feas}}}(\sigma)}\card{ \paren{ \sum_{W \in \ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{feas}}}(\sigma)} \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[W \mid \ensuremath{\Pi}_1, T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}]} - \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[W \mid T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}] \cdot \card{\ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{feas}}}(\sigma)}}\\
			&\leqslant \frac{x}2 \cdot \sum_{\sigma} \beta_{\sigma} + \frac1{\card{\ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{feas}}}(\sigma)}} \cdot\sum_{W \in \ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{feas}}}(\sigma)} \beta_{\sigma} \tag{by triangle inequality and definition of $\beta_{\sigma}$} \\
			&= \frac{x}2 \cdot \sum_{\sigma} 2 \beta_{\sigma} \\
			&=   \sum_{\sigma} \sum_{W \in \ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{feas}}}(\sigma)} \card{\ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[W \mid T, \ensuremath{\Pi}_1, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}] - \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[W \mid T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}]} \cdot \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[\sigma \mid T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}, W] \tag{by definition of $\beta_{\sigma}$ and $x$} \\
			&= \sum_{W} \card{\ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[W \mid T, \ensuremath{\Pi}_1, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}] - \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[W \mid T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}]} \sum_{\sigma: W \in \ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{feas}}}(\sigma)}  \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[\sigma \mid T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}, W] \\
			&=  \sum_{W} \card{\ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[W \mid T, \ensuremath{\Pi}_1, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}] - \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[W \mid T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}]} \cdot 1 \tag{$\ensuremath{\bm{\sigma}} \mid T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}, W$ is uniform over $\ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{feas}}}(\sigma)$, by part $(ii)$ and $(iii)$ of \Cref{obs:feasible-pair}} \\
			&\leqslant	2 \cdot \tvd{\ensuremath{\mathcal{G}}_p(\ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{spec}}}(G) \mid \ensuremath{\Pi}_1, T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}})}{\ensuremath{\mathcal{G}}_p(\ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{spec}}}(G) \mid T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}})}. \tag{by definition of total variation distance}

\begin{align*}
			&\ensuremath{{\mathbb{E}}}_{\sigma \mid \ensuremath{\Pi}_1, T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}}	\tvd{\ensuremath{\mathcal{G}}_p(\ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{spec}}}(G) \mid \ensuremath{\Pi}_1, T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}},\sigma)}{\ensuremath{\mathcal{G}}_p(\ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{spec}}}(G) \mid T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}, \sigma)} \\
			&= \frac{x}2 \cdot  \sum_{\sigma} \sum_{W \in \ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{feas}}}(\sigma)} \card{\ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[W \mid \ensuremath{\Pi}_1, T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}]- \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[W \mid T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}, \sigma ] \cdot \paren{ \sum_{W \in \ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{feas}}}(\sigma)} \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[W \mid \ensuremath{\Pi}_1, T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}]}} \\
			&\leqslant  \frac{x}2 \cdot  \sum_{\sigma} \sum_{W \in \ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{feas}}}(\sigma)} \Bigg(\card{\ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[W \mid \ensuremath{\Pi}_1, T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}]- \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[W \mid T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}]}\\
			&\hspace{6mm} + \card{\ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[W \mid T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}, \sigma ] \cdot \paren{ \sum_{W \in \ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{feas}}}(\sigma)} \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[W \mid \ensuremath{\Pi}_1, T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}]} - \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[W \mid T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}]}\Bigg) \tag{by triangle inequality}\\
			&\leqslant \frac{x}2 \cdot \sum_{\sigma} \beta_{\sigma} +  \sum_{W \in \ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{feas}}}(\sigma)}\card{\frac1{\card{\ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{feas}}}(\sigma)}} \cdot \paren{ \sum_{W \in \ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{feas}}}(\sigma)} \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[W \mid \ensuremath{\Pi}_1, T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}]} - \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[W \mid T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}]} \tag{by part $(iv)$ of \Cref{obs:feasible-pair}, and definition of $\beta_\sigma$} \\
			&\leqslant \frac{x}2 \cdot \sum_{\sigma} \beta_{\sigma}	+ \frac1{\card{\ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{feas}}}(\sigma)}} \cdot\sum_{W \in \ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{feas}}}(\sigma)}\card{ \paren{ \sum_{W \in \ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{feas}}}(\sigma)} \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[W \mid \ensuremath{\Pi}_1, T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}]} - \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[W \mid T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}] \cdot \card{\ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{feas}}}(\sigma)}}\\
			&\leqslant \frac{x}2 \cdot \sum_{\sigma} \beta_{\sigma} + \frac1{\card{\ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{feas}}}(\sigma)}} \cdot\sum_{W \in \ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{feas}}}(\sigma)} \beta_{\sigma} \tag{by triangle inequality and definition of $\beta_{\sigma}$} \\
			&= \frac{x}2 \cdot \sum_{\sigma} 2 \beta_{\sigma} \\

			&=  \sum_{W} \card{\ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[W \mid T, \ensuremath{\Pi}_1, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}] - \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[W \mid T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}]} \cdot 1 \tag{$\ensuremath{\bm{\sigma}} \mid T, \ensuremath{i^{\star}}, W$ is uniform over $\ensuremath{\textnormal{\textsc{feas}}}(\sigma)$, by part $(ii)$ and $(iii)$ of \Cref{obs:feasible-pair}} \\

First, we argue about $\ensuremath{i^{\star}}$, $T$, and $S_{\ensuremath{i^{\star}}}$. Distribution of $\ensuremath{i^{\star}}$ and $S_{\ensuremath{i^{\star}}}$ are the same in both cases by construction. For all $a\in[\ell]$ subset $C_{\ensuremath{i^{\star}}, a}$ of size $k^{p-1}$ is uniformly sampled from $S_{\ensuremath{i^{\star}}}$. As Bob samples $T$ such that $T \cap S_{\ensuremath{i^{\star}}} = C_{\ensuremath{i^{\star}}, i}$, and as set $C_{\ensuremath{i^{\star}}, i}$ is uniformly random from $S_{\ensuremath{i^{\star}}}$ of size $k^{p-1}$, set $T$ sampled by Bob has the same distribution as in $\ensuremath{\mathcal{G}}_p$.
		
		Now, we argue about the row $\ensuremath{i^{\star}}$ of matrix $x$. We have the following conditions:
		\begin{itemize}
			\item \textbf{Balance in $S_{\ensuremath{i^{\star}}}$:} The number of ones and zeros in the $r_p/4$ columns indexed by $S_{\ensuremath{i^{\star}}}$ must be equal in row $\ensuremath{i^{\star}}$. This is explicitly stated in protocol $\pi_{\textsc{index}}$. To see that such a row can be sampled, note that at most $\ell \cdot k^{p-1} = r_p/8$ co-ordinates in $S_{\ensuremath{i^{\star}}}$ are fixed due to step~\ref{item:row-istar-fix-by-Y} in $\pi_{\textsc{index}}$. Regardless of how biased these fixed values are, the remaining $r_p/8$ co-ordinates in $S_{\ensuremath{i^{\star}}}$ remain free and can be set appropriately to balance the number of zeroes and ones across the total $r_p/4$ columns of set $S_{\ensuremath{i^{\star}}}$.
			
			\item \textbf{Consistency in $S_{\ensuremath{i^{\star}}} \cap T$:} For all $j\in S_{\ensuremath{i^{\star}}}\cap T$, we want $x_{\ensuremath{i^{\star}}, j}$ to be equal. In protocol $\pi_{\textsc{index}}$, we have $x_{\ensuremath{i^{\star}}, j} = y_i$ for any $j \in C_{\ensuremath{i^{\star}}, i}$, and by construction $S_{\ensuremath{i^{\star}}} \cap T = C_{\ensuremath{i^{\star}}, i}$. Therefore, this condition is also satisfied. 
		\end{itemize}
		
		For all $j \in [t_p]$ where $j\neq \ensuremath{i^{\star}}$ the marginal distribution of $S_j$ and row $j$ of matrix $x$ are also the same as in $\ensuremath{\mathcal{G}}_p$ by the same reasoning. 
		The joint distribution of these random variables are also exactly as in $\ensuremath{\mathcal{G}}_p$ by the independence properties stated in \Cref{obs:rows-independent}.

For the first part of \Cref{thm:adv-res}, we use the construction in \Cref{prop:cpg-dense}. We know for all $k, n_a \geqslant 1$ such that $k=o(\sqrt{\log n_a})$ for all $2 < a \leqslant p$, there exists an $(r_a, t_a, k)$-cluster packing graph $G$ such that 
		\[
		r_a = \frac{n_a}{2^{\eta_r \cdot (\sqrt{\log n_a\cdot\log k})}} \quad \textnormal{and}  \quad
		t_a = \frac{n_a}{2^{\eta_t \cdot (\sqrt{\log n_a\cdot\log k})}},
		\]
		for some absolute constants $\eta_r, \eta_t$. 
		Starting from large enough $n_p=n$, we get constructions for all $3 \leqslant a < p$ with  $n_{a-1}=r_a/4$. Thus, by~\Cref{lem:adv-lb-cluster} we know that any deterministic $p$-player protocol $\pi$ that distinguishes between input graph $G$ with $\ensuremath{\chi}(G) \leqslant k\cdot p$ and $\ensuremath{\chi}(G)\geqslant k^p$ with probability at least  $2/3$ has communication cost at least 
		\begin{align}
			\Omega(1)\cdot \min_{2 \leqslant a\leqslant p} \{\frac{r_a\cdot t_a}{(a+1)^2\cdot k^{a-1}}\}
			&  = 	\Omega(1)\cdot \min_{2 \leqslant a\leqslant p}  \{\frac{(n_a)^2}{(a+1)^2\cdot k^{a-1} \cdot 2^{(\eta_r + \eta_t) \cdot (\log n_a \cdot \log k)^{1/2}}}\} \notag\\
		&	\geqslant \frac{(n_2)^2}{(p+1)^2 \cdot k^{p-1} \cdot 2^{(\eta_r + \eta_t) \cdot (\log n_p\cdot\log k)^{1/2}}}. \label{eq:interim-3}
		\end{align}
		This is because for each $2\leqslant a<p$, we have, 
		\[
			n_{a} = \frac{r_{a+1}}{4} = \frac{n_{a+1}}{2^{2 + \eta_r \cdot (\log n_{a+1} \cdot \log k)^{1/2}}} < n_{a+1}.
		\]
		To get \Cref{eq:interim-3}, we have taken the lowest numerator (corresponding to $a = 2$) and the largest denominator (corresponding to $a = p$). 
	
	We also have, 
	\begin{align}
		n_2 =\frac{r_3}{4} = \frac{n_3}{2^{2 + \eta_r \cdot (\log n_3 \cdot \log k)^{1/2}}} \geqslant \frac{n_p}{2^{p \cdot (2+\eta_r \cdot (\log n_{p} \cdot \log k)^{1/2})}},\label{eq:interim-4}
	\end{align}
	by using the bounds on parameters in \Cref{eq:params-all}.
	Putting \Cref{eq:interim-3} and \Cref{eq:interim-4} together, we get the lower bound on $p$-player deterministic communication protocol $\ensuremath{\pi}$ to be at least:
	\begin{align*}
CC(\ensuremath{\pi}) \geqslant \frac{n_p^2}{2^{2 \log (p+1) + (p-1) \log k + 2(p+1) \cdot (2 + (\eta_r + \eta_t) \cdot (\log n_p \cdot \log k)^{1/2})}} = \frac{n_p^2}{2^{\Theta(p \cdot \sqrt{\log k} \cdot (\sqrt{\log k} + \sqrt{\log n_p}))}}.
	\end{align*}
	
	Parameters $p, k$ obey $p \cdot \sqrt{\log k} = o(\sqrt{\log n_p})$ from statement of \Cref{thm:adv-res}, which gives the required lower bound that $CC(\ensuremath{\pi}) = n^{2-o(1)}$. 
	
	We just need to ensure that the value of $k$ satisfies the condition in \Cref{prop:cpg-dense} for all $2 \leqslant a \leqslant p$. That is, we  need $k = o(\sqrt{\log n_2})$, and this is true because $\log n_2  = \log n_p - o(\log n_p)$ because of from \Cref{eq:interim-4}.
	







		For the second part of \Cref{thm:adv-res}, we use the cluster packing graphs from ~\Cref{prop:cpg-large-r}.  We know for $n, k\geqslant 1$ such that $k=o(\frac{\log n}{\log \log n})$, there is a $(r, t, k)$-cluster packing graph $G$ with parameters 
		\[
		r=\frac{n}{2k^2}\cdot (1-o(1)) \quad \textnormal{and} \quad t = n^{\Omega(1/\log\log{n})}. 
		\]
		To get the properties of~\Cref{lem:adv-lb-cluster}, let $n_p=n$, $r_p=r$, and $t_p=t$.
		Then for all $3\leqslant a \leqslant p$ we set
		$n_{a-1} = \frac{r_a}{4}$, and $r_{a-1}, t_{a-1}$ based on $n_{a-1}$. 
		Thus, by~\Cref{lem:adv-lb-cluster} and starting from large enough $n$ we get the communication complexity lower bounded by
		\begin{align}
			\Omega(1)\cdot \min_{2 \leqslant a\leqslant p} \{\frac{r_a\cdot t_a}{(a+1)^2\cdot k^{a-1}}\}
			\geqslant \frac{n_2^{1+{\Omega(1/\log \log n_2)}}}{2k^{p+1} \cdot (p+1)^2}.\label{eq:interim-6}
		\end{align}
		This is because we have:
		\[
	n_{a-1} = \frac{r_a}{4} = \frac{n_a}{2k^2 \cdot 4} \cdot (1-o(1)) < n_a, 		
		\]
		for all $2 < a \leqslant p$, and the density $r_a \cdot t_a = n_a^{1+\Omega(1/\log \log n_a)}$ is increasing with $n_a$. 
		We also have:
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:interim-7}
			n_2 = \frac{n_3}{8k^2} \cdot (1-o(1)) \geqslant \frac{n_3}{9k^2} \geqslant \frac{n_p}{(9k^2)^p}.
		\end{equation}
		Hence, the lower bound in \Cref{eq:interim-6} becomes:
		\[
			CC(\ensuremath{\pi}) \geqslant \frac{n_p^{1+\Omega(1/\log (\log n_p - p \log k))}}{2^{\Theta(p \log k )}} = n_p^{1+\Omega(1/\log \log n_p)},
		\]
		for parameter $p \cdot \log k = o(\frac{\log n_p}{\log \log n_p})$, as in \Cref{thm:adv-res}. We just have to check if $k$ obeys the parameters required in \Cref{prop:cpg-large-r} for all $2 \leqslant a \leqslant p$. This is true because from \Cref{eq:interim-7}, we get $\log n_2 = \Omega(\log n_p - p \log k) = \Omega(\log n_p)$ based on the condition on parameters in the second part of \Cref{thm:adv-res}. 
		
		Lastly, by \Cref{prop:adv-communication-to-stream} and Yao's minimax principle, we can extend the lower bound to any streaming algorithm (either deterministic or randomized).

nodes.statement: Firstly, in each iteration i in [t], we have chi(Hii) leqslant chi(G) and thus the algorithm returns a chi(G)^t-coloring in the worst case. Moreover, under the coloring returned by~Crefalg:sparsification no edge in G setminus Mit+1 will be monochromatic: consider the iteration i in [t] wherein the edge e=(u,v) is removed from Mii; under the coloring Cii this edge is not monochromatic and so in the final coloring, the tuple of colors for u and v will be different (at least) in index i in [t]. We thus only need to prove that Mit+1 will be empty which implies the correctness of the algorithm immediately. The following claim shows that size of Mii drops by a factor of n^1/t in each iteration. With exponentially high probability, for every i in [t], \[ cardMii+1 leqslant n^-1/t cdot cardMii. \] Fix any function f: V rightarrow [n] as a `potential' coloring of the sampled graph Hii. Let M(f) denote the set of monochromatic edges in Mii under the coloring f. Suppose that cardM(f) > n^-1/t cdot cardMii; we show that with exponentially high probability f cannot be a proper coloring of Hii and then do a union bound over all choices of f to argue that the coloring Cii returned in this iteration cannot satisfy~Crefeq:multipass-contradiction, which implies the claim. Over the randomness of Hii from Mii, we have, ensuremathtextnormalPrparenf is a proper coloring of Hii &=ensuremathtextnormalPrparenno edge from M(f) is sampled\\ &leqslant prod_ein M(f)(1-ensuremathtextnormalPr(e sampled)) tagby the negative correlation of sampling without replacement\\ &leqslant expparen-sum_ein M(f)ensuremathtextnormalPr(e sampled) tagas 1-xleqslant e^-x for all xin[0, 1]\\ &= expparen-fraccardM(f)cardMii cdot n^1+1/t cdot logn \\ &leqslant expparen-fracn^-1/t cdot cardMiicardMii cdot n^1+1/t cdot logntagby~Crefeq:multipass-contradiction \\ &= expparen-nlogn leqslant n^-1.44n. A union bound over n^n possible choices of the coloring function f ensures that, with probability at least 1-n^-0.44n, any proper coloring f of Hii cannot satisfy~Crefeq:multipass-contradiction, hence the returned coloring Cii and Mii+1 satisfy the requirement of the claim, concluding the proof. rlapnobreak ifvmode relax else ifdimlastskip<1.5em hskip-lastskip hskip1.5em plus0em minus0.5em fi nobreak vrule height0.75em width0.5em depth0.25emfi_textnormal~~Crefclm:bound-on-monochromatic We can now finalize the proof of~Creflem:coloring-alg1. \begin{align*}
    \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}\paren{\text{$f$ is a proper coloring of $\Hi{i}$}}  &=\ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}\paren{\text{no edge from $M(f)$ is sampled}}\\
    &\leqslant \prod_{e\in M(f)}(1-\ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}(e\text{ sampled})) \tag{by the negative correlation of sampling without replacement}\\
    &\leqslant \exp\paren{-\sum_{e\in M(f)}\ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}(e\text{ sampled})} \tag{as $1-x\leqslant e^{-x}$ for all $x\in[0, 1]$}\\
    &= \exp\paren{-\frac{\card{M(f)}}{\card{\Mi{i}}} \cdot n^{1+1/t} \cdot \log{n}} \\
    &\leqslant \exp\paren{-\frac{n^{-1/t} \cdot \card{\Mi{i}}}{\card{\Mi{i}}} \cdot n^{1+1/t} \cdot \log{n}}\tag{by~\Cref{eq:multipass-contradiction}} \\
    &= \exp\paren{-n\log{n}} \leqslant n^{-1.44n}. 
\end{align*}

nodes.statement: For the purpose of analysis, for any i geqslant 1, define Mii as the monochromatic edges under the existing coloring C in iteration i of the for-loop in~Crefalg:random-order. Then, the randomness of the stream ensures that Hii is chosen uniformly from Mii (note that none of the edges in H_1,ldots,H_i-1 stored before iteration i or skipped due to not being monochromatic in C can be part of Mii). This is exactly as in~Crefalg:sparsification; the rest of~Crefalg:random-order is verbatim as~Crefalg:sparsification, hence the entire algorithm is a faithful simulation of~Crefalg:sparsification (technically speaking,~Crefalg:random-order may not finish reading the entire stream if the t iterations of the algorithm finishes before all edges of the stream arrive; however, this happens with exponentially small probability, since as shown in the analysis of~Crefalg:sparsification, the probability that Mit+1 neq emptyset is exponentially small). The correctness of the algorithm thus follows from~Creflem:coloring-alg1. As for the space, the algorithm only needs to store n^1+1/tlogn edges of the subgraph Hii for the current iteration i in [t], which only needs O(n^1+1/tlog^2n) space, and a coloring C which can be stored in O(nlogn) space (since we never need to use more than n colors and so each color can be stored in O(logn) bits). This concludes the proof.

For the purpose of analysis, for any $i \geqslant 1$, define $\Mi{i}$ as the monochromatic edges under the existing coloring $C$ in iteration $i$ of the for-loop in~\Cref{alg:random-order}.  
Then, the randomness of the stream ensures that $\Hi{i}$ is chosen uniformly from $\Mi{i}$ (note that none of the edges in $H_1,\ldots,H_{i-1}$ stored before iteration $i$ or skipped due to not being monochromatic in $C$ can be part of $\Mi{i}$). 
This is exactly as in~\Cref{alg:sparsification}; the rest of~\Cref{alg:random-order} is verbatim as~\Cref{alg:sparsification}, hence the entire algorithm is a faithful simulation of~\Cref{alg:sparsification} (technically speaking,~\Cref{alg:random-order} 
may not finish reading the entire stream if the $t$ iterations of the algorithm finishes before all edges of the stream arrive; however, this happens with exponentially small probability, since as shown in the analysis of~\Cref{alg:sparsification}, the probability that $
\Mi{t+1} \neq \emptyset$ is exponentially small). The correctness of the algorithm thus follows from~\Cref{lem:coloring-alg1}. 

As for the space, the algorithm only needs to store $n^{1+1/t}\log{n}$ edges of the subgraph $\Hi{i}$ for the current iteration $i \in [t]$, which only needs $O(n^{1+1/t}\log^2{n})$ space, and a coloring $C$ which can be stored in $O(n\log{n})$ space (since we never need
to use more than $n$ colors and so each color can be stored in $O(\log{n})$ bits). This concludes the proof.

This is exactly as in~Crefalg:sparsification; the rest of~Crefalg:random-order is verbatim as~Crefalg:sparsification, hence the entire algorithm is a faithful simulation of~Crefalg:sparsification (technically speaking,~Crefalg:random-order may not finish reading the entire stream if the t iterations of the algorithm finishes before all edges of the stream arrive; however, this happens with exponentially small probability, since as shown in the analysis of~Crefalg:sparsification, the probability that Mit+1 neq emptyset is exponentially small). nodes.statement: We can also directly implement~Crefalg:sparsification in t passes of adversarial streams and prove~Crefprop:multi-pass. Basically, implement each iteration of the algorithm by making a separate pass over the entire stream and sample n^1+1/tlogn edges from the monochromatic ones under the current coloring using reservoir sampling. The correctness and space complexity of this algorithm is verbatim as in~Creflem:alg-random-order and it also needs t passes at most, proving~Crefprop:multi-pass.

nodes.statement: Given a random partition E_A and E_B of G in the robust communication model, Alice and Bob can form the stream sigma = sigma_A circ sigma_B where sigma_A and sigma_B are random permutations of E_A and E_B, respectively. They can then run A on sigma exactly as in~Crefprop:stream-cc with O(s) communication and since sigma is a random permutation of E---given the random partitioning of E into E_A and E_B, and the individual random ordering of sigma_A and sigma_B---A solves P with the same probability of success as before, leading to the desired communication protocol.

Given a random partition $E_A$ and $E_B$ of $G$ in the robust communication model, Alice and Bob can form the stream $\sigma = \sigma_A \circ \sigma_B$ where $\sigma_A$ and $\sigma_B$ are random permutations of 
	$E_A$ and $E_B$, respectively. They can then run $A$ on $\sigma$ exactly as in~\Cref{prop:stream-cc} with $O(s)$ communication and since $\sigma$ is a random permutation of $E$---given the random partitioning of $E$ into $E_A$ and $E_B$, and 
	the individual random ordering of $\sigma_A$ and $\sigma_B$---$A$ solves $\mathbb{P}$ with the same probability of success as before, leading to the desired communication protocol.

nodes.statement: Let pi_textsccolor be a protocol in the robust communication model that distinguishes q-colorable from (q^2/4)-colorable graphs with probability of success at least 1-2^-q^4/4. Let graph G^* be a graph obtained by~Creflem:graph-simple for parameter k:=q/2, and let t=Omega(n^2/q^5) be the number of specified subgraphs in G^*. Let these subgraphs themselves be H_1, H_2, ldots, H_t. Now consider the Index^a,b_m problem of xin\0, 1\^t and iin [t] with parameters a = k cdot binomk2 textnormaland b = k^2 cdot binomk2. We design a protocol pi_textscindex for this problem using pi_textsccolor. newcommandxcopy[2]ensuremathx_#1^#2 newcommandicopy[1]ensuremathi^#1 We use the same reduction as in Crefalg:protindex-adv to construct the graph G = (V, E) on which protocol pi_textsccolor is run based on input x and i. It is useful to explicitly state this reduction for our purposes as the partitioning of the edges is different. The edges E will be: E_x &:= settextnormal edges of H_ell mid ell in [t], x_ell = 1, \\ E_i &:= set(u,v) mid u, vtextnormal are vertices in two different cliques in H_i,\\ E &:= E_x cup E_i. Protocol pi_textscindex for Index^a,b_t of x in set0,1^t and i in [t] given the protocol pi_textsccolor: ~vspace-0.5cm item For all jin [t], partition the edges of H_j between Alice and Bob using public randomness, ensuring that each player receives a number of edges in H_j equal to the number of copies of x_j they hold. If x_j=1, each player adds the chosen edges to the graph and if x_j = 0, the players keep H_j an entirely empty subgraph. item For index i, partition the edges of E_i between Alice and Bob using public randomness, ensuring that each player receives a number of edges in E_i equal to the number of copies of i they hold. item Let E_B be the edge set that Bob holds, and E_A be the edge set of Alice. item Alice runs protocol pi_textsccolor on G_A=(V, E_A) and sends the message M(G_A) to Bob. Bob continues to run protocol pi_textsccolor on edges E_B. item Bob outputs x_i=1 if pi_textsccolor declares chi(G)geqslant q^2/4 and otherwise outputs 0. We argue that each edge from the set E is present in exactly one of E_A, E_B with equal probability and independently of other edges. This will show that the partition of edges of E is uniformly random between the two players Alice and Bob, as required in the robust communication model. First we argue about edges in E_x. For each jin [t], where x_j=1, if Alice holds all copies of x_j then all of H_j goes to Alice's edges E_A, and if Bob holds all copies, then all of H_j goes to Bob's edges E_B. And, if Alice holds 0 < ell < a copies of x_j and Bob holds a-ell many of them, for each ein H_j either Alice gets this edge or Bob does (using the random partitioning with public randomness). In this case, for each edge e in H_j: \[ ensuremathtextnormalPrparenAlice receives e in H_j in E_A mid ell copies of x_j are sent to Alice = fraca-1 choose ell-1a choose ell, \] using the randomness of the partitioning via public randomness. Moreover, given the random partitioning of copies of x_j in Index^a,b_t, the probability that Alice receives ell copies of x_j is binomaell/2^a. Thus, in total the probability that Alice gets an edge ein H_j is ensuremathtextnormalPrparenAlice gets e in H_j = sum_ell=1^a fraca choose ell2^acdotfraca-1 choose ell-1a choose ell = frac12^a sum_ell=1^a a-1 choose ell-1 =frac12^acdot 2^a-1=frac12. The same holds for Bob. This same argument is true for E_i. Thus, all edges in E have been partitioned randomly in this reduction. The independence also follows by the independence across the copies of entries in (x,i) and the public randomness of players. The correctness of the reduction is already established in Creflem:two-player-robust. We get that the error probability of pi_textscindex is exactly the same as the error probability of pi_textsccolor. Thus, the probability of error of pi_textscindex is at most delta = 2^-q^4/4 leqslant 2^-(2k)^4/4 leqslant 2^-(a+b)/4 based on values of a, b in Crefeq:a-b-values . Thus, using~Crefprop:robust-index, we get CC(pi_textsccolor) geqslant CC(pi_textscindex)= Omega(t)cdot (4^-a+b) = Omega(n^2/(q^5 cdot 4^(2k)^4)) = Omega(n^2/(q^5 cdot 4^q^4)), concluding the proof.

\label{rem:sim-dynamic}
 	The definition of dynamic streams does \underline{not} limit the length of the stream nor the edge frequencies during the stream (only at the end). Almost all algorithms in the literature follow this definition 
	and the only exception we are aware of belongs to~\cite{KallaugherP20} for a rather non-standard problem. This definition allows one to use the characterization of~\cite{AiHLW16} (see also~\cite{LiNW14}) 
	in dynamic streams to prove lower bounds on space complexity of algorithms via a certain simultaneous communication model (see~\Cref{sec:sim}); this characterization is used 
	in many previous lower bounds (see, e.g.~\cite{Konrad15,WeinsteinW15,AssadiKLY16,AssadiKL17}) and we use it in this paper also. It remains an interesting 
	question to prove~\Cref{thm:dynamic-lower} without relying on the characterization of~\cite{AiHLW16} and thus possibly for shorter streams; see, e.g.~\cite{DarkK20} for more discussion on this topic.

Define 
	\[
		t := {\frac{p}{2\ln{n}}} \cdot \chi(G).
	\]
    	To prove this lemma we need the following claim, which shows that the inclusion of any one fixed vertex in the subgraph $H$ cannot increase
	its chromatic number by much (stochastically). 
     \begin{claim}\label{claim:prob-removingVertex}
        For a sampled subgraph $H$ as in~\Cref{lem:vertex-sample} and any vertex $v\in V$, we have
        \[
            \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}\Paren{\chi(H)< t \mid v\in H} \geqslant \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}\Paren{\chi(H)< t-1}.
        \]
     \end{claim}
     \begin{proof}
    Consider $H \setminus \set{v}$, the graph obtained by removing $v$ from $H$ (if it exists). Then
    \begin{align*}
        \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}\Paren{\chi(H) < t  \mid v \in H} \geqslant \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}\Paren{\chi(H \setminus \set{v}) < t-1 \mid v \in H} = \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}\Paren{\chi(H \setminus \set{v}) < t-1};
    \end{align*}
    here, the inequality holds because conditioned on $v \in H$ whenever $\chi(H \setminus \set{v}) < t-1$, we necessarily have $\chi(H) < t $ also since we can just color $v$ in $H$ using a different color than all of $H \setminus \set{v}$; 
    and, the equality holds because distribution of $H \setminus \set{v}$ is a random subset of $G \setminus \set{v}$ (by picking each vertex independently with probability $p$) regardless of whether or not $v \in H$. 
    Finally, as $\chi(H \setminus v) \leqslant \chi(H)$, 
    \[
        \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}\Paren{\chi(H \setminus \set{v}) < t-1} \geqslant \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}\Paren{ \chi(H) < t-1},
    \]
    proving the claim. \rlap{\nobreak \ifvmode \relax \else \ifdim\lastskip<1.5em \hskip-\lastskip \hskip1.5em plus0em minus0.5em \fi \nobreak \vrule height0.75em width0.5em depth0.25em\fi$_{\textnormal{~~\Cref{claim:prob-removingVertex}}}$}

    We now continue the proof of~\Cref{lem:vertex-sample}. 
    Suppose by contradiction that the lemma is false and thus we have, 
    \begin{align}\label{eq:prob-sample-contradiction}
    \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}\Paren{\chi(H) < t-1} > \frac{1}{2}.
    \end{align}      
    Define $\mu$ as the distribution of subgraph $H$ \emph{conditioned} on the event that $\chi(H) < t$ (we emphasize that this is $t$ and not $t-1$ unlike in~\Cref{eq:prob-sample-contradiction}). 
    Sample 
    \[
    	k := {\frac{2\ln{n}}{p}}
    \]
    independent subgraphs $H_1,\ldots,H_k$ from $\mu$ (by the lemma assumption, $k$ is an integer). We prove that there exist $k$ such sampled subgraphs that every vertex $v\in V$ has been sampled at least once among them and use this to properly color
    $G$ with less than $\chi(G)$ colors, a contradiction. 
        
    Consider any vertex $v \in V$ and any $i\in[k]$; we have,
    \begin{align*}
        \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}_{\mu}\Paren{v\in H_i} &= \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}\Paren{v \in H \mid \chi(H) < t} \tag{in RHS and throughout this part, $H$ is a subgraph sampled as in the lemma statement} \\
        &=\frac{\ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}} \Paren{v\in H} \cdot \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}\Paren{\chi(H)< t \mid v \in H}}{\ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}\Paren{\chi(H)< t}} \tag{by Bayes' rule}\\
        &\geqslant\frac{\ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}} \Paren{v\in H} \cdot \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}\Paren{\chi(H)< t-1}}{\ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}\Paren{\chi(H)< t}} \tag{by~\Cref{claim:prob-removingVertex} to drop the conditioning on $v \in H$}\\
        &> \frac{p}{2} \tag{by~\Cref{eq:prob-sample-contradiction} in the nominator and upper bounding denominator by one}. 
    \end{align*}
    So in sampling of $H_1,\ldots,H_k \sim \mu^k$, the probability that $v\in V$ is not sampled in any subgraph is
    \begin{align*}
    \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}_{\mu^k}\Paren{v \notin \cup_{i=1}^t H_i} &= \prod_{i=1}^{k} \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}_{\mu}\Paren{v \notin H_i} \tag{by the independence of samples $H_1,\ldots,H_t$} \\
    &< \paren{1-\frac{p}{2}}^{k} \tag{by the bound established in the previous equation} \\
    &\leqslant \exp\paren{-\frac{p}{2} \cdot \frac{2\ln{n}}{p}} \tag{by the choice of $k$ and since $1-x \leqslant e^{-x}$ for $x \in [0,1]$} \\
    &= \frac{1}{n}.



    \end{align*}
    Thus, by union bound over all vertices, we get that the probability of having a vertex that is not sampled is less than $1$ (given the strict inequality above). Thus, there exists a set of samples $H_1, \ldots, H_k$ such that every vertex shows up in at least one of 
    these samples. Moreover, we have that $\chi(H_i) < t$ for all $i \in [k]$. If we color each of these subgraphs using a distinct palette of colors (by assigning each vertex to any one of the subgraphs it appears in arbitrarily), 
    we obtain a proper coloring of $G$ with 
    \[
    	\sum_{i=1}^{k} \chi(H_i) < k \cdot t = \paren{\frac{2\ln{n}}{p}} \cdot \paren{\frac{p}{2\ln{n}} \cdot \chi(G)} = \chi(G), 
    \]
    namely, a proper coloring of $G$ with less than $\chi(G)$ colors, a contradiction with the definition of the chromatic number. Thus,~\Cref{eq:prob-sample-contradiction} cannot hold
    and we  conclude the proof of \Cref{lem:vertex-sample}.

Thus, if chi(G) leqslant q, the algorithm deterministically outputs `small' as none of its subgraphs can have chi(H_i) > q. On the other hand, if chi(G) geqslant q cdot t, then, by~Creflem:vertex-sample, for any i in [k], we have, \[ 1/2 geqslant ensuremathtextnormalPrparenchi(H_i) < fracp2lnn cdot chi(G) -1 = ensuremathtextnormalPrparenchi(H_i) < frac4lnn2lnn cdot t cdot q cdot t -1 geqslant ensuremathtextnormalPrparenchi(H_i) leqslant q. \] Hence, the probability that none of the trials output `large' is at most (1/2)^k = 1/n^2, meaning that with high probability, in this case, the algorithm outputs `large'. This proves the correctness. We now bound the space complexity of the algorithm. The algorithm requires storing each V_i which, with high probability, can be stored in O(n/t cdot log^2n) bits (by doing the sampling implicitly first and then storing the name of sampled vertices explicitly which with high probability are at most O(n/t cdot logn) many). It also requires storing each H_i which involves maintaining leqslant cardV_i^2 counters with O(log^2n) bits each, for a total of O(n^2/t^2 cdot log^4n) bits for each H_i. Given the algorithm stores O(logn) choices of V_i and H_i, we obtain the final bound on the space as well.

Since \emph{final} multiplicities of edges in $G$ are promised to be $\mbox{\rm poly}(n)$ and we are maintaining a counter mod $n^{\log{n}}$ in the algorithm, each $H_i$ will be 
	the induced subgraph of $G$ on $V_i$. Thus, if $\chi(G) \leqslant q$, the algorithm deterministically outputs `small' as none of its subgraphs can have $\chi(H_i) > q$. 
	On the other hand, if $\chi(G) \geqslant q \cdot t$, then, by~\Cref{lem:vertex-sample}, for any $i \in [k]$, we have, 
	\[
		1/2 \geqslant \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}\paren{\chi(H_i) < \frac{p}{2\ln{n}} \cdot \chi(G) -1} = \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}\paren{\chi(H_i) < \frac{4\ln{n}}{2\ln{n} \cdot t} \cdot q \cdot t -1} \geqslant \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}\paren{\chi(H_i) \leqslant q}. 
	\]
	Hence, the probability that none of the trials output `large' is at most $(1/2)^k = 1/n^2$, meaning that with high probability, in this case, the algorithm outputs `large'. This proves the correctness. 
	
	We now bound the space complexity of the algorithm. The algorithm requires storing each $V_i$ which, with high probability, can be stored in $O(n/t \cdot \log^2{n})$ bits (by doing the sampling implicitly first and then storing the name of sampled vertices explicitly which with high probability are at most $O(n/t \cdot \log{n})$ many). It also requires storing each $H_i$ which involves maintaining $\leqslant \card{V_i}^2$ counters with $O(\log^2{n})$ bits each, for a total of $O(n^2/t^2 \cdot \log^4{n})$ bits for each $H_i$. Given the algorithm stores $O(\log{n})$ choices of $V_i$ and $H_i$, 
	we obtain the final bound on the space as well.

For all $j\in [t]$, let $\rv{Y}_j:=(\rv{X}_{1,j}, \ldots, \rv{X}_{p,j})$, where for each $i\in [p]$, the random variable $\rv{X}_{i,j}$ denotes the $j$-th entry $x_{i,j}$ in the input row vector of player $P_i$. We are going to upper bound the LHS of~\Cref{claim:sketching-omega(1)} 
    in the following. By the definition of conditional mutual information, 
    \[
        \mi{\rv{\Theta}}{\rv{\Pi} \mid \ensuremath{\bm{\sigma}} ,\rv{J}} = \ensuremath{{\mathbb{E}}}_{j\in [t]} \bracket{\mi{\rv{\Theta}}{\rv{\Pi} \mid \ensuremath{\bm{\sigma}} , \rv{J}=j)}} = \frac{1}{t} \sum_{j=1}^t \mi{\rv{Y}_j}{\rv{\Pi} \mid \ensuremath{\bm{\sigma}} , \rv{J}=j},
    \]
    where the last equality holds since $\rv{J}$ is uniform over $[t]$ and when $\rv{J}=j$, for all $i \in [p]$, each $x_{i,j}$ is set to be $\theta$. This implies $\rv{\Theta}$ is fixed by $\rv{Y}_{j}$ and vice-versa conditioned on $\rv{J}=j$. Continuing the equations, we have,
    \begin{align}
       \mi{\rv{\Theta}}{\rv{\Pi} \mid \ensuremath{\bm{\sigma}} ,\rv{J}} &=\frac{1}{t} \sum_{j=1}^t \mi{\rv{Y}_j}{\rv{\Pi}_1,\ldots,\rv{\Pi}_p \mid \ensuremath{\bm{\sigma}} , \rv{J}=j} \tag{by the equation above and $\rv{\Pi} = (\rv{\Pi}_1,\ldots,\rv{\Pi}_p)$} \\
        &=\frac{1}{t} \sum_{j=1}^t \sum_{i=1}^p \mi{\rv{Y}_j}{\rv{\Pi}_i \mid \rv{\Pi}_{1},\ldots,\rv{\Pi}_{i-1}, \ensuremath{\bm{\sigma}} , \rv{J}=j} \tag{by the chain rule of mutual information (\Cref{fact:it-facts}-(\ref{part:chain-rule})\xspace)}\\
        &= \frac{1}{t} \sum_{j=1}^t \sum_{i=1}^p \mi{\rv{X}_{i,j}}{\rv{\Pi}_i \mid \rv{\Pi}_{1},\ldots,\rv{\Pi}_{i-1}, \ensuremath{\bm{\sigma}} , \rv{J}=j} \tag{as $\rv{X}_{i,j}$ uniquely determines $\rv{Y}_j$ and vice versa conditioned on $\rv{J}=j$} \\ 
        &\leqslant \frac{1}{t} \sum_{j=1}^t \sum_{i=1}^p \mi{\rv{X}_{i,j}}{\rv{\Pi}_i \mid \ensuremath{\bm{\sigma}} , \rv{J}=j}, \label{eq:ref-later}
    \end{align}
    where we prove the inequality of~\Cref{eq:ref-later} in the following. We claim that 
    \[
    	\rv{\Pi}_i \perp \rv{\Pi}_{1},\ldots,\rv{\Pi}_{i-1} \mid \rv{X}_{i,j}, \ensuremath{\bm{\sigma}},\rv{J}=j,
    \]
    which allows us to apply~\Cref{prop:info-decrease} to drop the conditioning on $\rv{\Pi}_1,\ldots,\rv{\Pi}_{i-1}$ and increase the mutual information term above, hence proving~\Cref{eq:ref-later}. The stated independence holds
    because conditioned on $\rv{X}_{i,j},\ensuremath{\bm{\sigma}},\rv{J}=j$, the randomness in the input of each player $i \in [p]$ is that of $x_{i,j'}$ for $j' \neq j^*=j$, which is chosen independently across the players; hence, 
    the messages of the players that are functions of these randomness (conditioned on the above terms) are also independent.

\]

The edge set E will be specified later. The vertex set V is partitioned into k layers of n/k vertices each, namely Li1, ldots, Lik. Each layer Lii is further partitioned into n/(k cdot r) groups of size r each, denoted by Lij_1, ldots, Lii_r. Inside each group Lii_j, the r vertices are denoted by vijij_1, ldots, vijij_r. For each \[ b in [fracn2k cdot r], p in [fracn2k^2 cdot r], s in [r], \] we define a geometric line here as: \[ P_b, p, s = parenvij1b_s, vij2b+p_s, ldots, vijkb+(k-1) cdot p_s. \] By our choice of parameters, \[ b + (k-1) cdot p leqslant fracn2k cdot r + (k-1) cdot fracn2k^2 cdot r leqslant fracnk cdot r, \] hence all the points on all the lines are valid points in G. We will now define the edges set E of G. For each line P_b,p,s, we add all the edges between the k many vertices in the line to form a k-clique. For b in [n/(2kr)], p in [n/(2k^2cdot r)], we define subgraph H_b,p as a k-cluster of size r by making all k many vertices in each line P_b,p,s as a k-clique for all s in [r]. This construction closely follows the one in \Cref{lem:graph-simple}, except that we use groups of size $r$ instead of $k$ now. 
	
	We create a graph $G = (V, E)$ on $n$ vertices. The edge set $E$ will be specified later. 
The vertex set $V$ is partitioned into $k$ layers of $n/k$ vertices each, namely $\Li{1}, \ldots, \Li{k}$. Each layer $\Li{i}$ is further partitioned into $n/(k \cdot r)$ groups of size $r$ each, denoted by $\Li{j}_1, \ldots, \Li{i}_r$. Inside each group $\Li{i}_j$, the $r$ vertices are denoted by $\vij{i}{j}_1, \ldots, \vij{i}{j}_r$. 

For each
\[
	b \in [\frac{n}{2k \cdot r}], \qquad p \in [\frac{n}{2k^2 \cdot r}], \qquad s \in [r],
\]
we define a geometric line here as:
\[
	P_{b, p, s} = \paren{\vij{1}{b}_s, \vij{2}{b+p}_s, \ldots, \vij{k}{b+(k-1) \cdot p}_s}. 
\]
By our choice of parameters, 
\[
	b + (k-1) \cdot p \leqslant \frac{n}{2k \cdot r} + (k-1) \cdot \frac{n}{2k^2 \cdot r} \leqslant \frac{n}{k \cdot r},
\]
hence all the points on all the lines are valid points in $G$. 

We will now define the edges set $E$ of $G$. For each line $P_{b,p,s}$, we add all the edges between the $k$ many vertices in the line to form a $k$-clique. 
For $b \in [n/(2kr)], p \in [n/(2k^2\cdot r)]$, we define subgraph $H_{b,p}$ as a $k$-cluster of size $r$ by making all $k$ many vertices in each line $P_{b,p,s}$ as a $k$-clique for all $s \in [r]$. 
All the lines are vertex-disjoint, and thus subgraph $H_{b,p}$ is a $k$-cluster of size $r$. 

The total number of these subgraphs is $b \cdot p = \frac{n^2}{4k^3 \cdot r^2}$, as required. The inducedness property follows similarly as in the proof of \Cref{lem:graph-simple}.

nodes.name: Proof of \Cref{prop:cpg-dense}
nodes.statement: We start with a DUP-graph ensuremathG_textscdup with the parameters given in Crefprop:dup. We use a p cdot q family ensuremathH of (k, k)-layered graphs H_i,j for i in[q], j in [p], all of which are k-cliques. We will show that G = ensuremathtextnormaltextscembed(ensuremathH rightarrow ensuremathG_textscdup) is a (p, q, k)-cluster packing graph. Let H_i be the subgraph induced by all the edges added to G via the UPC ensuremathP_i = (P_i,1, ldots, P_i,p), for each i in [q]. Each edge added to G is added with respect to some path P_i,j, and thus is a part of subgraph H_i. The edges in these subgraphs H_i for i in [q], therefore, form a partition of the edge set of G. Each subgraph H_i consists of vertex-disjoint union of H_i,1, ldots, H_i,p by Creflem:embed-induced, and each H_i,j for j in [p] is a k-clique by construction. Hence, each subgraph is a k-cluster of size p. Creflem:embed-induced also proves that the subgraph H_i does not contain edges from any other subgraph H_i', as it states that the subgraph induced by the edges of H_i contains no other edges apart from those in H_i. Thus, edges of graph G can be partitioned into q-many induced k-clusters of size p. The parameters p = r and q = t are the same as in the statement of the proposition, which completes the proof.
